concepts.headline: 6 of 7 Ultrasonic Cleaners Leave Live Bacteria
concepts.persona: Denture caregiver (daughter): Megan, 45, freight dispatcher from Toledo, Ohio, caring for her widowed 83-year-old father Arthur in Erie, Pennsylvania.
concepts.primary_text:
My dad still had that chipped 1994 Ford picnic mug on his bathroom sink on Christmas Eve.

It was half full of cloudy water.

His lower denture sat at the bottom like a pale plastic jaw, surrounded by a gray ring of scum.

I should have dumped it right then. Instead, I just went to bed.

Three weeks later, I was sitting in an intensive care waiting room in Erie, watching a machine breathe for him.

Let me back up.

I am Megan, forty-five, a freight dispatcher in Toledo.

My dad, Arthur, is eighty-three, a retired tool-and-die maker in Erie, Pennsylvania.

Mom passed away last spring, and he lives alone on Raspberry Street.

When I visited for Christmas, he looked gray and worn out.

At night, through the wall, I heard this wet, rattling cough start at two in the morning.

In the morning, the water in his mug smelled like sour swamp grass.

He had spent eight dollars a box on Efferdent tablets for six years.

He had cheap drugstore brushes that scratched the acrylic, and a thirty dollar pod from an online ad that quit after two weeks.

Nothing stopped the yellow film.

In January, Dad was rushed to the emergency room with a 103-degree fever.

Both lungs were flooded. The doctor diagnosed severe aspiration pneumonia.

Sitting by his bed, I felt this sick dread. I was right there over Christmas and never checked that mug.

I called my cousin Keith, a respiratory therapist in Cleveland.

Keith asked if Dad slept in his dentures or soaked them in open water.

When I said yes, Keith told me that is where the pneumonia started.

In sleep, swallow and cough reflexes weaken. Bacteria pool on the plate and trickle down the windpipe into the lungs.

Acrylic is porous like an unglazed coffee mug. Biofilm burrows deep inside the microscopic scratches where tablets cannot reach.

A 2015 study by Iinuma in the Journal of Dental Research proved seniors sleeping in dentures had more than double the pneumonia risk.

Keith told me to run a fingernail along the inside ridge. If it feels slick and smells sour, that is living bacterial biofilm.

He said Dad needed four things: forty-two thousand Hertz ultrasonic waves, medical-grade ultraviolet light, tap water only, and a five-minute cycle.

That night in the waiting room, I ordered the DentalPULSE Pod.

When Dad finally came home, we set it on his counter, filled the stainless steel tank with warm tap water, and pressed start.

Within sixty seconds, tiny clouds of grayish debris started rising off the pink acrylic.

After one five-minute cycle, the water was murky, yellowish-brown.

Dad stared into that basin like he had seen a ghost.

Years of trapped bacterial slime and old food grime had shaken completely out of the microscopic pores.

The plate looked clear again, without that greasy white film along the gumline.

Within three days, his foul morning breath was gone.

The rattling cough through the wall stopped completely.

He slept through the night without choking, and his appetite came roaring back.

He told me his mouth finally felt clean instead of sour and coated.

Now he pops his dentures in every evening while he washes his face, pushes one button, and goes to bed with clear airways.

That chipped 1994 Ford mug is not sitting on his bathroom sink anymore.

It sits on his basement workbench, holding rusty drill bits.

On his bathroom counter sits the clean white pod.

Soaking in a cloudy cup and scrubbing with a plastic brush was slowly poisoning his lungs.
